title: Imprinting and Microdeletions: Prader-Willi, Angelman, Williams and WAGR
summary: Learn how parent of origin at 15q11q13 separates Prader-Willi from Angelman syndrome, why a deletion is only one of several mechanisms and methylation testing confirms both, and how the 7q11.23 (Williams-Beuren) and 11p13 (WAGR) contiguous deletions present and are detected.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 71 Hit 9 (Prader-Willi vs Angelman), Hit 12 (Williams syndrome), Hit 15 (WAGR 11p13) and Trap 6 (PWS and Angelman are different deletions). Checked against the EMQN/ACGS 2019 guideline (Beygo 2019), Angulo 2015, Bird 2014, Honjo 2015, Collins 2024, Stephens 2024, Hol 2021, Duffy 2021 and Marcato 2014. Qualifications: the reviewer frames PWS/AS as one “15q11.2 deletion”; sources give the region as 15q11q13 and show deletions are only 70–75% of cases, so the lesson teaches all mechanisms and methylation testing (rv-pws-as-mechanisms). The reviewer calls Williams an “ELN deletion”; sources describe a ~1.55 Mb, ~28-gene contiguous deletion including ELN (rv-williams-contiguous-deletion). The reviewer’s “~1 in 3 children with aniridia develop Wilms tumor” was not found; sources give a 45–60% risk in WAGR and no risk with isolated PAX6 deletion, so the lesson does not teach the 1-in-3 figure (rv-wagr-aniridia-wilms). Kozel 2021 (Nat Rev Dis Primers) could not be read: Europe PMC full text returned a server error and the PMC page showed a captcha. Not taught: management, growth hormone, Bloom syndrome.

objectives: Explain how genomic imprinting at 15q11q13 makes parent of origin decide between Prader-Willi and Angelman syndrome.
List the molecular mechanisms of each syndrome and explain why DNA methylation analysis confirms both but misses UBE3A variants.
Recognise the Williams-Beuren (7q11.23) and WAGR (11p13) contiguous deletions, their key features and how they are detected.

scenes.title: Four children, four missing pieces
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: four referrals reach the cytogenetics bench — (1) a floppy newborn with a poor suck; (2) a 3-year-old with seizures, no words and frequent laughter; (3) an infant with a heart murmur from narrowing just above the aortic valve and a high serum calcium; (4) a newborn with absent irises (aniridia). Question token: “Which piece is missing — and does it matter which parent it came from?”

cues.text: Four referrals reach the cytogenetics bench: a floppy newborn who cannot suck well, and a three-year-old with seizures, no words and frequent laughter.
Then an infant with narrowing just above the aortic valve and a high calcium, and a newborn born without irises.
Which piece of which chromosome is missing, and does it matter which parent it came from?

props.label: Which piece is missing — and from which parent?

scenes.title: Imprinting at 15q11q13
scenes.altText: Schematic: the paternal and maternal copies of chromosome 15 at band 15q11q13, side by side. An imprinting centre controls the region. On the paternal copy, several genes are switched on (SNRPN, MAGEL2, NDN and snoRNA genes); their maternal copies are methylated and silent. On the maternal copy, UBE3A is the gene expressed in neurons; in brain the paternal UBE3A is silent. Lose the paternal-only genes → Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS). Lose maternal UBE3A function → Angelman syndrome (AS).

cues.text: Most genes work from both copies. A cluster at chromosome fifteen, band q11 to q13, is imprinted: some genes there work only from one parent’s copy, under the control of an imprinting centre.
Genes such as SNRPN, MAGEL2 and NDN work only from the father’s copy. Their copies on the mother’s chromosome are methylated and silent.
UBE3A is the reverse. In neurons it works only from the mother’s copy.
So losing the father’s genes causes Prader-Willi syndrome, and losing the mother’s UBE3A causes Angelman syndrome. Parent of origin decides the disease.

scenes.title: Deletion is only one way to lose a copy
scenes.altText: Two mechanism cards from the 2019 EMQN/ACGS best-practice guideline. PWS: de novo paternal 15q11q13 deletion 70–75%; maternal uniparental disomy (UPD) 25–30%; imprinting defect about 1%. AS: de novo maternal deletion about 75%; UBE3A variant 5–10%; imprinting defect about 3%; paternal UPD 1–2%; no abnormality found 10–15%. Test card: DNA methylation analysis at 15q11q13 detects deletion, UPD and imprinting defect in PWS — fully methylated (maternal-only pattern) in PWS, unmethylated (paternal-only pattern) in AS; methylation-specific MLPA adds copy number to show a deletion. It does not detect UBE3A sequence variants.

cues.text: The two syndromes share a region, but a deletion is only one way to lose a parent’s contribution. In Prader-Willi, about seventy to seventy-five percent have a paternal deletion, and twenty-five to thirty percent have two maternal copies of chromosome fifteen: maternal uniparental disomy.
In Angelman, about seventy-five percent have a maternal deletion. Others have a UBE3A variant, an imprinting defect, or two paternal copies, and some have no change found.

Deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects all leave an abnormal methylation pattern, so DNA methylation analysis is the key test. Prader-Willi shows only the maternal, methylated pattern; Angelman shows only the paternal, unmethylated pattern.

Methylation-specific MLPA adds copy number, so it also shows whether a deletion is the cause. An Angelman patient with a normal methylation result may still have a UBE3A variant, which needs sequencing.

lines: MS-MLPA adds copy number; misses UBE3A variants

scenes.title: Two more missing pieces: 7q11.23 and 11p13
scenes.altText: Williams-Beuren syndrome card: a contiguous gene microdeletion at 7q11.23, about 1.55 Mb in roughly 90% of patients, in a region of about 28 genes that includes ELN (elastin). Elastin hemizygosity drives the arteriopathy, mainly supravalvar aortic stenosis; also hypersocial behaviour, visuospatial weakness, and hypercalcaemia that can be severe in neonates. Usually de novo. Detected by FISH, MLPA or chromosomal microarray — the deletion is not visible on conventional karyotyping. WAGR card: contiguous deletion at 11p13 that must include both WT1 and PAX6; Wilms tumour risk 45–60%; isolated PAX6 deletions carry no Wilms tumour risk; in one 30-year registry series median age at Wilms diagnosis was 22 months and 37.5% had bilateral disease. Hook answers: (1) PWS, (2) AS, (3) Williams-Beuren, (4) aniridia — check whether WT1 is deleted.

cues.text: Williams-Beuren syndrome is a contiguous gene deletion at seven q eleven point two three. About ninety percent have the same one point five five megabase deletion, in a region of about twenty-eight genes that includes the elastin gene, ELN.

Losing one elastin copy explains the arterial narrowing, mainly supravalvar aortic stenosis. Patients are typically hypersocial, with weak visuospatial skills, and some infants have high calcium. The deletion is too small for a routine karyotype, so FISH, MLPA or microarray finds it.

WAGR is a contiguous deletion at eleven p thirteen that removes both WT1 and the aniridia gene PAX6. Wilms tumour risk is forty-five to sixty percent, but a deletion of PAX6 alone carries no Wilms risk.
Back to the hook: Prader-Willi, Angelman, Williams-Beuren, and an aniridia baby whose Wilms risk depends on whether WT1 is deleted too.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “PWS and Angelman are different deletions” (✓ same 15q11q13 region; parent of origin decides — and many cases are not deletions at all); “A normal deletion FISH rules out PWS” (✓ FISH misses UPD and imprinting defects; methylation analysis is the confirming test); “Every child with aniridia has a high Wilms risk” (✓ the risk comes with WT1 deletion, as in WAGR; an isolated PAX6 deletion carries none).

cues.text: Trap one: Prader-Willi and Angelman are different deletions. No: the deleted region is the same. Which parent lost it decides the syndrome, and many cases are not deletions at all.
Trap two: a normal FISH rules out Prader-Willi. No: FISH sees deletions only. Uniparental disomy and imprinting defects need methylation analysis.
Trap three: every child with aniridia has a high Wilms risk. No: the risk comes with a WT1 deletion, as in WAGR. A PAX6 deletion alone carries none.

scenes.title: Whose copy is missing?
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Prader-Willi = no Pa’s copy; Angelman = no Ma’s copy.” Whether the missing copy was deleted or replaced by the other parent’s duplicate (UPD), ask whose copy is absent. Tokens: Pa missing → Prader-Willi · Ma missing → Angelman · 7 = elastin heart · 11 = eye + kidney. A card lists where the aid breaks (imprinting defects, UBE3A variants, and the rule not applying to Williams or WAGR).

cues.text: Memory aid: Prader-Willi means no Pa’s copy; Angelman means no Ma’s copy. Deleted or replaced by a second copy from the other parent, just ask whose copy is absent. Then seven is the elastin heart, and eleven is the eye and the kidney.

Where it breaks: in imprinting defects both copies are present but one is silenced; Angelman can come from a UBE3A variant with a normal methylation pattern; and the Pa and Ma rule does not apply to Williams or WAGR.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Imprinting defect: copy present but silenced
Williams, WAGR: Pa/Ma rule does not apply

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “15q11q13: no paternal contribution → Prader-Willi · no maternal UBE3A → Angelman · confirm by methylation”, “7q11.23 (ELN) → Williams-Beuren · 11p13 WT1 + PAX6 → WAGR with Wilms risk”.

cues.text: At 15q11q13 the missing parent decides the syndrome, with Prader-Willi when the father’s genes are lost and Angelman when the mother’s UBE3A is lost, so confirm by methylation, while Williams-Beuren and WAGR are contiguous deletions found by FISH, MLPA or microarray.

props.label: 15q11q13: no paternal → PWS · no maternal UBE3A → AS · methylation

explanation.what: Plain language: at one spot on chromosome 15, some genes only work from the father’s copy and one only works from the mother’s copy. Losing the father’s working genes gives Prader-Willi syndrome; losing the mother’s gives Angelman syndrome. Other syndromes come from losing a small stretch of several neighbouring genes, such as Williams-Beuren on chromosome 7 and WAGR on chromosome 11. Scientific terms: genomic imprinting, imprinting centre, 15q11q13, SNRPN, UBE3A, uniparental disomy (UPD), imprinting defect, DNA methylation analysis, methylation-specific MLPA (MS-MLPA), contiguous gene deletion, ELN hemizygosity, supravalvar aortic stenosis, WT1, PAX6.
explanation.why: Imprinted genes are silenced by methylation on one parental copy, so the working copy depends on parent of origin. Any mechanism that removes the only working copy (deletion, uniparental disomy, imprinting defect, or for UBE3A a point variant) causes disease. In contiguous deletions, the phenotype is the sum of the lost genes: elastin loss narrows arteries in Williams-Beuren, and WT1 loss adds Wilms tumour risk in WAGR.
explanation.measure: PWS: paternal deletion 70–75%, maternal UPD 25–30%, imprinting defect ~1%. AS: maternal deletion ~75%, UBE3A variant 5–10%, imprinting defect ~3%, paternal UPD 1–2%, unexplained 10–15%. Methylation analysis diagnoses PWS in more than 99% and separates PWS (maternal-only, methylated) from AS (paternal-only, unmethylated); MS-MLPA adds copy number. Williams-Beuren: ~1.55 Mb deletion in ~90%, ~28 genes; FISH, MLPA or CMA. WAGR: Wilms risk 45–60%; isolated PAX6 deletion, no Wilms risk.
explanation.differs: PWS (neonatal hypotonia, poor suck, later hyperphagia and obesity) vs AS (absent speech, seizures, ataxia, happy demeanour with easily provoked laughter). Deletion vs UPD vs imprinting defect vs UBE3A variant. Williams-Beuren (supravalvar aortic stenosis, hypersocial) vs WAGR (aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, Wilms tumour).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: match parent of origin to syndrome, pick the test that detects UPD (methylation, not FISH), match 7q11.23 to elastin and supravalvar aortic stenosis, and recognise that Wilms risk in aniridia depends on WT1 deletion.

questions.stem: A hypotonic newborn with a poor suck has a normal FISH study for the 15q11q13 deletion. Prader-Willi syndrome is still suspected. Which test is most appropriate next?

options.rationale: Correct. Methylation analysis detects PWS from deletion, maternal UPD or an imprinting defect.

options.text: Repeat FISH with the same probe
options.rationale: Incorrect. FISH detects only deletions; maternal UPD (25–30% of PWS) gives normal FISH.
Incorrect. Maternal UPD gives normal cytogenetic findings, and an imprinting defect needs no DNA sequence change, so a karyotype cannot show either.
Incorrect. UBE3A variants cause Angelman syndrome, not PWS.

questions.stem: A child has absent speech, seizures, ataxia and a happy demeanour with easily provoked laughter. A 15q11q13 deletion is found. On which parental chromosome is the deletion?

options.rationale: Correct. This is Angelman syndrome: loss of the maternally expressed UBE3A.
Incorrect. A paternal deletion causes Prader-Willi syndrome.

options.text: Either; parent of origin does not matter
options.rationale: Incorrect. The region is imprinted, so parent of origin decides the syndrome.
Incorrect. Angelman deletions are heterozygous, on the maternal copy.

questions.stem: An infant has supravalvar aortic stenosis, hypercalcaemia and later a very sociable personality. Which finding best fits?

options.text: A 7q11.23 microdeletion including ELN, shown by FISH, MLPA or microarray
options.rationale: Correct. This is Williams-Beuren syndrome; elastin loss drives the arteriopathy.

options.text: An 11p13 deletion including WT1 and PAX6
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is WAGR: aniridia, genitourinary anomalies and Wilms tumour risk.

options.text: A deletion visible on routine G-banded karyotype
options.rationale: Incorrect. The 7q11.23 microdeletion is not visible on conventional karyotyping.

claims.text: Imprinted 15q11q13: paternal-only genes (SNRPN, MAGEL2, NDN, snoRNAs) and maternal-only UBE3A in neurons; paternal loss → PWS, maternal loss → AS.
Mechanism proportions for PWS and AS.

Methylation analysis detects deletion, UPD and imprinting defects, separates PWS from AS, and cannot give subtype alone; MS-MLPA adds copy number; UBE3A variants need sequencing; FISH is a dosage (deletion) test; maternal UPD gives normal cytogenetic findings.
Clinical features of PWS and AS.
Williams-Beuren: ~1.55 Mb 7q11.23 contiguous deletion including ELN; SVAS from elastin hemizygosity; hypersocial, visuospatial weakness, hypercalcaemia; FISH/MLPA/CMA detection.
claims.note: Honjo 2015 gives the 28 genes for the 1-2 Mb 7q11.23 region, not for the 1.55 Mb deletion itself. Marcato 2014 states the microdeletion is not visible by conventional karyotyping.

claims.text: WAGR: 11p13 deletion of WT1 and PAX6; Wilms risk 45–60%; isolated PAX6 deletion no Wilms risk.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 71 Hit 9 and Trap 6 present PWS and Angelman as the “SAME 15q11.2 deletion”. The EMQN/ACGS 2019 guideline gives the region as 15q11q13 and shows deletion in only 70–75% of PWS and ~75% of AS; maternal UPD (25–30% of PWS), imprinting defects and UBE3A variants also cause disease, so methylation analysis, not deletion FISH, is the confirming test (register flag rv-pws-as-mechanisms).

Ch. 71 Hit 12 calls Williams syndrome an “ELN deletion”. Sources describe a ~1.55 Mb contiguous deletion of about 28 genes including ELN; ELN changes alone cause SVAS without the full syndrome (register flag rv-williams-contiguous-deletion).

Ch. 71 Hit 15 says “~1 in 3 children with aniridia develop Wilms tumor”. No source read gives this figure; Hol 2021 gives a 45–60% risk in WAGR (WT1 + PAX6 deleted) and no Wilms risk with isolated PAX6 deletion. The lesson teaches the source figures (register flag rv-wagr-aniridia-wilms).
